summary: Describes the requirements, architecture, and interfaces of the ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse, between the clearinghouse and domain name registries and registrars. It covers provisioning and management of domain names during Sunrise and Trademark Claims periods for new top-level domains.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a new neighborhood opens for sale, a list of famous brand names is kept so brand owners get first dibs and others get a warning.

questions: how do sunrise periods work for domains
how does tmch protect brand names
when is the trademark claims period
subtitle: Interfaces and data formats for trademark protection during new domain launches.

tldr.problem: When ICANN launches new generic top-level domains (gTLDs), trademark holders need protection from others registering their brand names. Yet registries and registrars need standardized ways to coordinate with a central clearinghouse.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9361 defines the Trademark Clearinghouse (TMCH) system with two main periods: Sunrise gives trademark holders priority to register matching domains, and Trademark Claims notifies others when they try. It specifies interfaces, data formats, and processes for registries, registrars, and the clearinghouse to exchange information about domain registrations.
tldr.outcome: The TMCH system has been operational for over a decade, protecting more than 500,000 trademark records during new gTLD launches and providing a model other registries now follow.

today: RFC 9361 is an operational specification for a production system that continues to support domain trademark protection during all new gTLD launches. The Trademark Clearinghouse processes hundreds of new gTLDs and manages records for the vast majority of ICANN-recognized trademarks, making it a de facto standard for trademark protection in domain registration.

sections.title: Trademark Protection During Domain Launches
sections.content:
When ICANN introduces a new generic top-level domain (gTLD) such as .music or .shop, trademark owners face a risk: others could register domain names matching their brands. The ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse (TMCH) solves this problem with two special periods.

The Sunrise Period grants trademark owners an advance opportunity to register domain names matching their marks before the domain becomes available to the general public. The Trademark Claims Period follows Sunrise and runs for at least the first 90 days of general registration. During this time, anyone attempting to register a domain matching a recorded trademark receives a notification displaying the relevant mark information before the registration completes.

This RFC specifies the technical requirements, architecture, and interfaces between the TMCH and domain registries and registrars to implement these protections consistently across all new gTLDs.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new neighborhood opens for houses, the government lets famous brands claim their street names first. Then when anyone else tries to use those names, they get a warning note. This document explains how that system is technically built.

sections.title: System Architecture and Actors
sections.content:
The TMCH system involves multiple independent actors that must coordinate reliably. A Trademark Validator (TMV) is an ICANN-approved entity that authenticates and validates trademark records, ensuring they meet registration, court validation, or statutory protection requirements. The Trademark Database (TMDB) is a central repository that stores validated trademark records and provides information to registries and registrars. Domain registries operate the technical infrastructure for a specific TLD and manage domain registration. Registrars are accredited service providers that accept domain registration requests from end users and submit them to registries.

The architecture uses two types of periods with different information flows. During Sunrise, registries validate cryptographic Signed Mark Data (SMD) tokens issued by TMVs, while the TMDB publishes SMD Revocation Lists to prevent use of revoked credentials. During Trademark Claims, registries and registrars fetch lists of protected domain labels from the TMDB and present Trademark Claims Notices (TCNs) to registrants when matches occur. All domain registrations matching protected marks are reported back to the TMDB within 26 hours so trademark holders can be notified.
sections.plainLanguage: A Trademark Validator is like a government office that confirms a brand is real. The Trademark Database is a central filing cabinet. Registries and Registrars are like the salespeople at the domain store. During Sunrise, the store checks special signed tokens. During Claims, the store shows a warning note.

sections.title: Sunrise and Trademark Claims Procedures
sections.content:
During the Sunrise Period, a trademark holder presents their SMD token (issued by a TMV) to a registrar when registering a domain matching their mark. The registrar forwards this to the registry, which performs validation checks: confirming the SMD signature is valid, the TMV certificate is current and not revoked, the SMD has not expired, and the requested domain matches a label within the SMD. If all checks pass, the domain is registered and reported to the TMDB. The registry refreshes the SMD Revocation List at least every 24 hours to ensure revoked SMDs are rejected.

During the Trademark Claims Period, when a registrant requests a domain matching a protected trademark label, the registry provides a lookup key to the registrar. The registrar uses this key to fetch the Trademark Claims Notice from the TMDB, displays it to the registrant, and only proceeds with registration after the registrant acknowledges the notice. The registry validates that the TCN is current and has been acknowledged within the required time window (typically 48 hours), then reports the registration to the TMDB. The TMDB processes these reports within 30 minutes and notifies the affected trademark holders.
sections.plainLanguage: In Sunrise, you show your trademark certificate and register right away if it's valid. In Claims, the store shows you a warning and asks you to acknowledge it before allowing registration. Then the database tells the brand owner someone registered their name.

sections.title: Data Exchange Formats
sections.content:
The TMCH uses standardized CSV and XML formats for all data exchange. The Domain Name Label (DNL) List is a CSV file published twice daily by the TMDB, containing all domain labels covered by protected trademarks. Each entry includes the label, a unique lookup key, and the insertion datetime. Registries download this list at least every 24 hours to support Trademark Claims.

The SMD Revocation List is a CSV file similarly published twice daily, containing identifiers of revoked Signed Mark Data tokens. Registries and registrars download this at least every 24 hours and check it before accepting SMDs during Sunrise.

The List of Registered Domain Names (LORDN) is uploaded by registries to the TMDB at least daily. For Sunrise registrations, it includes the domain name, SMD identifier, registrar ID, and registration datetime. For Trademark Claims, it includes the domain name, Trademark Claims Notice identifier, and the datetime when the registrant acknowledged the notice. The TMDB validates each LORDN file within 30 minutes and returns a log file with result codes indicating success, warnings, or errors for each domain reported.
sections.plainLanguage: The system exchanges lists of protected names (updated twice a day), lists of revoked certificates (updated twice a day), and reports of registered domains (sent by registries, processed within 30 minutes).

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
Before participating in the TMCH system, each registry and registrar must complete a bootstrapping process. They receive authentication credentials (typically per-TLD for registries), provide IP addresses for access control, and fetch the ICANN TMCH Certificate Authority trust anchor. They also receive the TMDB's PGP public key for cryptographically verifying the integrity of downloaded lists.

Communication uses HTTPS with HTTP Basic authentication for registry-to-TMDB and registrar-to-TMDB connections. All CSV files are PGP-signed to prevent tampering. The system is designed to handle high scale: registries can upload LORDN files concurrently, the TMDB publishes updated lists twice daily, and registrars can cache Trademark Claims Notices to minimize lookups during peak registration activity.

The system also supports an optional Qualified Launch Program (QLP) Period for additional registry-controlled launch activities. During QLP, registries apply either Sunrise or Trademark Claims rules based on whether domain registrations match the Sunrise List and/or DNL List, with special handling for domains registered outside the standard periods.
sections.plainLanguage: Before joining, each registry and registrar gets credentials and security certificates. They exchange encrypted lists and reports every day. There's also an optional launch period where registries can define custom rules.

sections.title: Operational Status
sections.content:
RFC 9361 is an informational specification describing a production system that has been operating since the 2012 gTLD expansion. The TMCH has processed registrations for hundreds of new gTLDs and holds records for over 500,000 protected trademarks. The specification has proven stable in deployment; RFC 9361 itself incorporates lessons learned from the initial implementation.

The document is not a standards-track RFC, reflecting that the TMCH is primarily an ICANN operational system rather than an Internet Standard. However, it serves as normative guidance for all registries and registrars participating in new gTLD launches, and other IP registries (such as the IRT for internationalized top-level domains) have modeled similar systems based on these specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: This system has been working since 2012 for hundreds of new domain extensions and protects over 500,000 brand names. It's a live system that ICANN runs, documented here so everyone knows exactly how it works.
